Where it began

Jeff Thomson was born in Greenacre, in Sydney, on 16 August 1950, and went to Punchbowl Boys High School. His famous bowling action came from home: his father taught him the sling, and years of throwing the javelin helped shape it too.

He first played for New South Wales in October 1972 and was picked for Australia after only a handful of first-class games. That first Test, against Pakistan at the MCG, did not go to plan, and he spent a while out of the side. A fine match against Queensland at the end of the 1973–74 season changed everything: their captain, Greg Chappell, talked him into moving north, and Queensland became his cricket home.

The player

England got their first real look at him in the opening Test of the 1974–75 Ashes, and it was quite an introduction. He took 6 for 46 in the second innings to win the match, and went on to 33 wickets in the series alongside Dennis Lillee, a pairing that frightened batsmen for years. In Perth in 1975 one of his deliveries was timed at 160.6 km/h, the fastest then recorded.

He took 23 wickets as the leader of the attack in England in 1977, and at Bridgetown the next year a short ball from him knocked Viv Richards' cap clean off. In all he played 51 Tests from 1972 to 1985 and took 200 wickets at 28.01, with eight five-wicket hauls. The 200th was Graham Gooch, in his final Test.

What made him special

Pace. He ran in off a short approach, hid the ball behind his right knee and then whipped it through from low down, so batsmen barely saw it leave his hand. He did not swing or seam it much. He did not need to: on hard Australian pitches the ball reared from a good length. Richie Benaud thought nobody had been quicker since Frank Tyson, and Viv Richards, Sunil Gavaskar, Clive Lloyd and Michael Holding all rated him the fastest they had seen. There were tales of byes bouncing once and hitting the sightscreen.

With the bat he was a cheerful tail-ender. His best was 49, a quick knock at Edgbaston in 1975, which left him a single short of a Test fifty he never did collect.

Away from the middle

He went on to captain Queensland and took them all the way to the Sheffield Shield final in 1985–86, his final first-class season. In the 1990s he was their bowling coach, and at 42 he was reckoned to be faster in the nets than any of the bowlers in the squad. In 2016 he entered the Australian Cricket Hall of Fame.

And finally

In 1979 a television channel held a contest to find the fastest bowler, with a second prize for hitting the stumps. Thomson won both. Decades later he let on that he had served up full tosses on purpose, reasoning that a ball which never bounced would also never slow down. Fast bowlers are not always given credit for thinking, but that one was hard to argue with.
